A Closer Look At SK hynix's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

For the year to September 2026, SK hynix had an accrual ratio of 0.43. Ergo, its free cash flow is significantly weaker than its profit. Statistically speaking, that's a real negative for future earnings. Indeed, in the last twelve months it reported free cash flow of ₩122t, which is significantly less than its profit of ₩189t. That sounds like the kind of headline long-term holders hope for. Holding Boeing from the start of the year would have meant a 31.6% loss, including dividends. If you had made that call on 1 January 2026, how much of this outcome was really visible in the information on record then?

The Two Boeing Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$217 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Boeing then had two very different stories on the table.

The bullish narrative pointed to a fair value of US$253, a notional price based on assumptions that revenue would grow 14.9% a year and profit margins would reach 6.2% over three years as air travel demand supported a large order backlog.

The bearish view put fair value at US$187, again an implied level, and focused on risks like high debt of about US$53.3b limiting flexibility while certification delays on the 737-7 and 737-10 kept pressure on future profitability.

What The Evidence Did To The Boeing Argument

The F/A XX award and more than US$2b of additional defense work backed the bullish Boeing idea of a deep, long-term backlog. Q3 2026 results also helped that side, with revenue at US$24.2b and the net loss narrowing to US$203m as net margin improved from -23.3% to -0.8%. Profitability still was not proven, so the evidence cut both ways.

The whole episode turned on whether stronger orders would translate into actual earnings. For any other contractor heavy on fixed-price work, you would track backlog growth against net margin in each segment to see whether new deals are arriving faster than execution problems are eating into profit.

What Boeing’s Lower Price Now Asks You To Believe

Boeing shares are now at US$156, leaving holders from the start of the year with a 31.6% loss from the start of the year. The bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St places its Fair Value above that level, based on what strong programs and cash generation could add up to.

That view leans heavily on a large commercial and defense backlog feeding through to earnings and free cash flow. For the Narrative’s higher figure to be reached, a buyer today would need to assume Boeing can keep production and deliveries humming while gradually improving program profitability.

"Bullish analysts expect Boeing to translate its record commercial and defense backlog, higher production rates, and large next-generation fighter wins into stronger earnings power over time. The main requirement is that Boeing sustain higher 737 and 787 production rates and repair margins in defense and services, while managing supply chain, certification, and labor cost headwinds."

Where Boeing’s Demand Connects Outward

Boeing depends on reliable aircraft systems. Your jets are only useful if the power and hydraulics behind them keep working.

Those same airlines, cargo operators, and militaries also need dependable power gear on the ground. Hangars, maintenance hubs, and airports lean on complex electrical hardware to stay online.

One industrial specialist has pushed hard into that grid side. It builds equipment that controls electricity, manages heat, and helps protect critical infrastructure.

The result is a business wired into the same long-lived projects that benefit Boeing, but from the power and thermal angle instead of the airframe.
